title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
statement:
You're given an unsorted list of integers, `nums`. Return the length of the longest run of consecutive integers (each one exactly 1 more than the one before) whose members all appear in `nums`. The numbers do not have to be next to each other in the list, or in order.

A value that appears several times counts once. For an empty list the answer is 0. Aim for O(n) time, which rules out sorting.

Constraints: 0 <= len(nums) <= 100,000; -10^9 <= nums[i] <= 10^9.

examples.explanation: 29, 30, 31 is a run of 3, and 5, 6, 7, 8 is a run of 4, so the answer is 4.
An empty list has no run at all.
Repeated values count once, so the longest run is just [9].

hints: What does 'consecutive' mean for a single value x? Which other values would extend a run through x?
Sorting makes runs easy to see but costs O(n log n). Can you check for the neighbours x - 1 and x + 1 without sorting?
A set answers 'is this value present?' in O(1). If you count upward from every value in the set, what is the worst case?
How can you tell in O(1) that a value is the start of a run rather than the middle of one? Only count from those.
Put the numbers in a set. For each x with x - 1 not in the set, walk x + 1, x + 2, ... while they are present and track the longest run.
followUps: What are the time and space complexity, and why isn't the inner while loop making it O(n^2)?
How would a sort-based solution work, and when would you accept it?
What if the numbers arrive as a stream and you need the longest run after every number?
How would you return the run itself instead of only its length?
idealAnswerPoints: Stores the numbers in a set for O(1) membership checks, which also removes duplicates
Starts counting only from values whose predecessor (x - 1) is absent
Extends each run by checking successive values in the set
Argues each number is visited a constant number of times, giving O(n) overall
Handles the empty list and duplicates, and can describe the sort-based alternative
weakAnswerSigns: Sorts the list and scans, without acknowledging that it is O(n log n)
Starts counting from every element, which is O(n^2) on a long run
Forgets duplicates and counts a repeated value twice
Scans the list instead of a set to check membership

rubric.correctness: Correct for empty input, duplicates, negatives, extreme values, scattered runs and one long run.
rubric.efficiency: O(n) expected time with a set and run-start check; sorting is O(n log n) and should be named as such.
rubric.code_quality: A clear start-of-run condition and a simple while loop, with no repeated work on the same run.
rubric.communication: Explains why only run starts are expanded and gives a concrete argument for the linear bound.
